item.title: A high-speed railway traces the legacy of the Long March
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
A high-speed railway traces the legacy of the Long March At Yan'an Railway Station, an Ansai waist drum troupe welcomes the launch of a direct high-speed rail service linking Ruijin in east China's Jiangxi province and Yan'an in northwest China's Shaanxi province on Sept. 6, 2026. (Photo/Liu Yijiang) The journey from Ruijin in east China's Jiangxi province to Yan'an in northwest China's Shaanxi province has changed dramatically over time. In the past, the Chinese Workers' and Peasants' Red Army soldiers, driven by a profound sense of mission, trekked roughly 12,500 kilometers across China wearing straw sandals, forging a path to survival through the arduous Long March. Today, the two cities are directly linked by a high-speed railway. The 1,857-kilometer journey takes just 11 hours and 32 minutes, offering a smooth and efficient travel experience. This year marks the 90th anniversary of the successful conclusion of the Long March. A single train ticket now bridges not only two distant cities but also two distinct eras. The transformation from a desperate struggle for survival to an ongoing drive for regional revitalization mirrors the sweeping transformations China has experienced. Aboard the train are descendants of Red Army soldiers, carrying straw sandals and certificates commemorating fallen martyrs as they travel to Yan'an on behalf of relatives who sacrificed their lives during the Long March. Other passengers, inspired by the Long March spirit, have embarked on this red-themed journey across thousands of kilometers. During the Long March, both Ruijin and Yan'an served as vital centers of China's revolutionary cause. The Red Army soldiers crossed snow-capped mountains and vast grasslands, broke through successive enemy blockades and paved the way forward with blood and sacrifice. They fought to save a war-torn China and secure a life of independence and happiness for the people. Today, those simple aspirations of earlier days have come to fruition. The poverty and isolation that once defined these regions have given way to vibrant communities and renewed economic vitality. Ruijin has steadily cultivated distinctive industries, including precision manufacturing, design-focused toy production, and textiles, while continuously improving public services and living standards. In Yan'an, apple cultivation has evolved from a modest agricultural activity into a major economic pillar. Environmental restoration has accompanied this growth, lifting fruit farmers out of poverty and transforming the city into a thriving community characterized by ecological health, industrial vitality, and improved livelihoods. The development of Ruijin and Yan'an offers a vivid example of how former revolutionary base areas are revitalizing. This transformation extends far beyond the two cities. Jinggangshan, an old revolutionary base in Jiangxi, has shaken off poverty by developing red tourism and leveraging its ecological resources. Xibaipo, also an old revolutionary base in north China's Hebei province, is promoting the integrated development of agriculture, culture, and red tourism, improving the quality of life for residents. In the Dabie Mountains, seven counties and county-level cities across three provinces have formed an alliance to develop red tourism, charting a new course for regional growth. Across China, former revolutionary base areas are steadily advancing toward shared prosperity. Photo shows a rural road in Ridong township, Ruijin, east China's Jiangxi province. (Photo/Zhu Haipeng) What has driven these transformations? The answer may lie in the roads themselves. A road construction plan dating back to 1933, preserved in Ruijin, reflects revolutionary forebears' hopes for roads that would connect communities and bring peace and prosperity. Today, an extensive network of national transportation corridors connects urban and rural areas and links mountains with the sea, reaching major revolutionary landmarks such as Ruijin, Zunyi in Guizhou province, and Yan'an. The vision of convenient travel for people and smooth flows of goods is steadily becoming a reality. The transformation from having no way forward to a vast network of well-connected roads reflects more than improvements in physical infrastructure. At its heart is the vitality of the path China has chosen: one rooted in the country's realities, attuned to the needs of the times and supported by its people. This path provides a solid foundation for revitalizing former revolutionary base areas and advancing national rejuvenation. The roads have been paved, yet the march continues. China is embarking on a "new Long March," with new challenges to overcome: repeated setbacks in laboratories, critical technological bottlenecks across industrial supply chains, and the many risks and challenges on the path to high-quality development. The tougher the challenges, the more important it is to draw strength from the spirit of the Long March, a precious spiritual legacy. The Long March National Cultural Park extends across 15 provincial-level regions along the route of the epic expedition, bringing history to life at former revolutionary sites and helping visitors connect with Long March stories. Here, history is no longer confined to static exhibits; it has become a living source of inspiration. By inspiring people through red-themed resources and passing the revolutionary legacy down through generations, China is forging a profound connection between the aspirations of the past and the achievements of today, drawing lasting spiritual strength for the "new Long March." Tourists visit an exhibition hall for the Zunyi Meeting in Zunyi, southwest China's Guizhou province. (Photo/Yuan Fuhong) Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: China Haul: Why foreign visitors are now leaving with full suitcases
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
China Haul: Why foreign visitors are now leaving with full suitcases Foreign visitors once left China with little more than a handful of souvenirs. Now many arrive with empty suitcases and leave with them packed. On TikTok, the trend has a name: China Haul. "China Haul" has become a new trend on social media platforms such as TikTok, in which foreign visitors unpack the items they bought in China and offer shopping suggestions to their audiences. South African creator Grace Mondlana filmed herself unboxing her haul—ranging from carefully designed cultural pieces to snacks—and the video pulled in more than 500,000 likes. The food account "Oh Yummy" walked into a snack shop in Changsha, central China's Hunan Province, stared at shelves lined with thousands of options, and called China a "snack paradise." That video surpassed 3 million views. Drones, foldable phones, and AI glasses turn up just as frequently. What used to be the occasional tourist souvenir has turned into serious shopping, and the range of products foreign visitors can buy in China keeps growing. This is no longer rare. From AI glasses at electronics market in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, to Chinese-style clothing and beauty products in shopping malls in east China's Shanghai, and from folding fans and fragrant sachets at riverside shops in Suzhou, southeast China's Jiangsu Province to herbal teas and cultural goods in boutiques in southwest China's Chongqing, it has become commonplace to see foreign tourists arriving with empty suitcases and leaving with fully packed luggage. Empty suitcases in, full suitcases out "Bring extra luggage for a shopping spree in China" has become common advice among foreign visitors. During the 2026 National Day holiday, China recorded 15.46 million inbound and outbound trips, averaging 2.21 million a day, up 6.7 percent year on year, according to the National Immigration Administration. In the first half of the year, 22.914 million foreign nationals entered China, a 20.4 percent year-on-year increase, with 77.7 percent of them arriving visa-free. Tech products dominate their shopping lists. Data from the Huaqiangbei Subdistrict in Shenzhen shows that nearly 8,000 foreign merchants have come to Huaqiangbei for procurement every day this year. As of July 2026, AI products made up 61 percent of electronics products in the commercial zone, a sharp jump from 41 percent in 2025. Overall AI-product sales in Huaqiangbei grew more than 55 percent year-on-year, while AI glasses sales doubled, and drone and robot sales rose 60–70 percent, according to a CCTV report. Cultural and creative products rooted in Chinese aesthetics come next. Suzhou's Pingjiang Road historic district is lined with intangible-heritage shops where visitors can buy Su embroidery fans and sachets—or try making them on the spot. Items such as loquat paste with fritillary bulb and moxibustion tools have been nicknamed "Chinese miracle remedies" by overseas users. Local fashion is the latest draw. At PANE, a Shanghai-based footwear brand, foreign customers account for 30 percent of foot traffic and 35 percent of sales. Chinese pop culture brand Pop Mart reported 37.12 billion yuan in revenue for 2025, with overseas sales making up more than 40 percent. Domestic beauty brands are also gaining ground: Florasis became the first Chinese beauty brand to enter Ulta Beauty, a major U.S. retailer. Why "China Haul" is catching on Looking at the recent "China+" trends on overseas social media, "China Haul" makes more sense. During the "China Travel" phase, people mostly filmed the scenery. In the "Chinamaxxing" period, they started recording high-speed trains, night markets, and drone deliveries—stuff that felt like a high-tech, slightly futuristic China. Now with "China Haul," they're actually packing their suitcases. Seeing it, going there, and bringing something home is what makes the impression stick. Once the products end up in someone's daily life—used, unboxed on camera, and flooded with "link please" comments—they stay familiar and gradually build trust. China's opening up policies have helped sustain the trend. China now offers unilateral visa-free entry to citizens of 50 countries and 240-hour visa-free transit to those of 57 countries. In the first half of 2026, the number of foreign travelers claiming departure tax refunds rose 366 percent year-on-year, while both refundable sales and the refund amounts themselves grew 69 percent. The "2.0 version" departure tax refund policy introduced in May 2026 extended the "refund upon purchase" window to 28 days nationwide before departure and introduced paperless processing with mutual recognition across locations. The continuous upgrading and expanding variety of Chinese products is the other major driver. Motivation has shifted from "because it's cheap" to "because it's good." Chinese manufacturing and design—backed by solid quality, distinctive Chinese aesthetics, and emotional resonance—continue to generate desire among overseas consumers. From the old staples of tea, silk, and panda plush toys to AI glasses, domestic running shoes, iconic cultural landmarks, and the loquat paste that foreign creators now call a "Chinese miracle remedy," the shopping experience for foreigners in China has become far richer. Suitcases packed to capacity and the rise of "China Haul" illustrate both the appeal of Chinese manufacturing and the practical results of China's continued opening. item.title: China's Central Archives opens over 5,000 Long March items to mark 90th anniversary
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
China's Central Archives opens over 5,000 Long March items to mark 90th anniversary China's Central Archives opens more than 5,000 Long March-related archival items to the public on October 19, 2026 to mark the 90th anniversary of the Red Army's Long March victory. Photo: CCTV News China's Central Archives opened more than 5,000 Long March-related archival items to the public on Monday to mark the 90th anniversary of the Red Army's Long March victory, offering firsthand accounts of key battles, strategic decisions and solidarity between soldiers and civilians, according to China Central Television (CCTV) News. The newly accessible materials mainly date from October 1934 to October 1936, including include programs and declarations issued by the Communist Party of China, Red Army telegrams and reports on operational deployments, and revolutionary newspapers and periodicals founded and published by the Party. Together, they showcase the revolutionary spirit of the CPC and the people's armed forces, vividly depicting how the Red Army and ordinary people stood united, braved sacrifice and pressed ahead during the Long March, according to CCTV News. Among the materials opened to the public for the first time is Jiebao (victory bulletin), a newspaper founded by the CPC's Shanghai central bureau. A total of 40 issues were published between October 1933 and June 1935, exposing the reactionary rule of the Kuomintang, publicizing the Red Army's military achievements and development in the revolutionary base areas. Liu Kun, a staff member of the Central Archives' archival access department, was cited as saying that "the December 17, 1934, issue of Jiebao carried a report stating, 'The westward-bound Red Army has victoriously captured Liping in Guizhou' … Liping was the site of the first Political Bureau meeting held by the CPC Central Committee after the Long March began. The Liping Meeting affirmed the decision to change course at Tongdao and established the Red Army's strategy of advancing westward, thereby averting the risk of being encircled and annihilated by Kuomintang forces had it continued north." The words "utmost urgency" on the telegram testify to the critical military situation at the time. Another document, titled "Report on the first division's covering of the entire army's bridge crossing tomorrow," provides a detailed account of the Red Army's exploits in capturing Luding Bridge, said Liu. "The capture of Luding Bridge was one of the major victories of strategic significance during the Red Army's Long March," Liu said. "As a firsthand battlefield record, this document details when units of the first red army corps arrived at Luding Bridge and launched their attacks. It also records the situation on the ground as they captured the bridge, defeated a regiment of Sichuan troops and seized military supplies. The document states, 'Today, we captured more than 100 prisoners and over 100 firearms, along with enough ammunition and hand grenades to substantially replenish our supplies.'" The 25th Red Army set out from Hejiachong in Luoshan county, Henan Province, on November 16, 1934, and arrived in Yongping, Shaanxi Province, on September 15, 1935, to become the first Red Army force to reach northern Shaanxi during the Long March. A special report submitted to the CPC Central Committee on July 17, 1935, by Wu Huanxian, the political commissar of the 25th Red Army, is an important historical source for research into the force's Long March. "In this report, Wu perceptively raised the question of whether they could join forces with the 26th and 28th armies, concentrate their strength to destroy enemy forces, support the main Red Army's operations in the northwest, and swiftly establish a new, strong and consolidated revolutionary base there," Liu said. "Operating in isolation, without instructions from the CPC Central Committee or deployments ordered by higher authorities, the CPC Hubei-Henan-Shaanxi Provincial Committee resolutely decided that the main force of the 25th Red Army should advance westward and northward to support the main Red Army. Wu's report also explains the thinking behind that decision," Liu said. Starting Monday, audiences can consult these materials at the Central Archives' public reading hall by presenting valid identification, such as a national ID card or work ID, per CCTV News. item.title: China leads the world in innovation clusters
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
China leads the world in innovation clusters A talent cooperation and exchange conference for the Yangtze River Delta G60 Science and Technology Innovation Corridor is held in Jinhua, east China's Zhejiang province, April 28, 2026. (Photo/Huang Wenlong) The World Intellectual Property Organization (WIPO) recently released its 2026 ranking of the world's top 100 innovation clusters. China accounted for 25 clusters on the list, ranking first globally for the fourth consecutive year. The Shenzhen-Hong Kong-Guangzhou, Beijing, and Shanghai-Suzhou clusters all ranked among the top 10. The ranking identifies regions with concentrated innovation activity based on indicators including international patent applications, scientific publications, and venture capital transactions. China's consistent strong showing on the list, with innovation clusters flourishing across multiple regions, demonstrates both the scale and depth of its innovation ecosystem. This leadership reflects years of strategic investment in coordinated regional tech development. Regional innovation networks have become a key pillar of the national innovation framework and provide a vital foundation for building China into a leading country in science and technology. Coordinated development in the Beijing-Tianjin-Hebei region has fostered deeper collaboration, with Beijing focusing on research and development while Tianjin and Hebei translate research findings into manufacturing applications. Meanwhile, the integrated development of the Yangtze River Delta has strengthened links among innovation hubs along the G60 Science and Technology Innovation Corridor, creating a cross-regional collaborative innovation platform spanning nine cities. Stronger regional collaboration has cultivated a sound pattern of innovation with multiple hubs working in concert. Beyond sheer numbers, the rankings also signal a comprehensive upgrade across China's broader innovation system. Innovation clusters capture the close links among research institutions, businesses, talent, and investment. In recent years, China has accelerated the commercialization of scientific and technological advances while nurturing and expanding new quality productive forces. Many of the innovation clusters on the list are also major industrial hubs. Wuhan in central China's Hubei province, ranked 17th, saw the value added of its industrial enterprises above the designated size in high-tech manufacturing rise 65.7 percent year on year in the first half of this year, as its optoelectronics and information technology industries gathered pace. Ningde in Fujian province, meanwhile, climbed 24 places in the rankings, driven in large part by innovation in its power battery industry. Photo shows the DeepBlue Technology Park in Dapeng New District, Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong province. (Photo/Li Jianqiang) This virtuous cycle between innovation and development is enabling more emerging and future-oriented industries to gain momentum and grow rapidly within these clusters. China's leading position in the number of top 100 global innovation clusters is also creating valuable opportunities for global partners. An increasing number of foreign-invested companies are choosing to conduct research and pursue innovation in China, with many establishing R&D centers in these clusters. In the first seven months of this year, foreign applicants filed more than 42,000 invention patent applications in China. In 2025, foreign investment actually utilized in scientific research and technical services accounted for nearly 1/5 of China's total utilized foreign investment. China is also committed to sharing the benefits of innovation through openness and cooperation. In the first half of this year, Chinese developers of innovative drugs reached 81 licensing deals with overseas partners, while industrial robots made in China were exported to 141 countries and regions. As Carsten Fink, WIPO's chief economist, noted, Chinese innovation is pushing the frontiers of global science and technology across an expanding range of fields, with countries around the world increasingly benefiting from it. Photo shows Taicang Biomedical Industrial Park in east China's Jiangsu province. (Photo/Ji Haixin) Today, global innovation resources are increasingly converging on China through its innovation clusters. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.

item.title: Chinese premier says ready to expand cooperation with Tajikistan in emerging industries
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
Chinese premier says ready to expand cooperation with Tajikistan in emerging industries DUSHANBE, Oct. 19 (Xinhua) -- Chinese Premier Li Qiang said Monday that China is willing to expand cooperation with Tajikistan in emerging industries such as the digital economy and artificial intelligence. In his meeting with Tajik President Emomali Rahmon, Li said China stands ready to expand bilateral trade with Tajikistan, strengthen cooperation in infrastructure, green minerals, connectivity and other fields, so as to jointly build new drivers of economic growth. He called for deepening cooperation with Tajikistan in law enforcement and security, saying both sides should strengthen intelligence exchanges and information sharing, jointly combat the three forces of terrorism, separatism and extremism, and safeguard lasting peace and stability in the region. The Chinese premier expressed hope that the Tajik side will continue to take strong measures to ensure the safety and security of Chinese personnel and enterprises in Tajikistan. Li arrived here on Sunday for an official visit to Tajikistan and the 25th meeting of the Council of Heads of Government (Prime Ministers) of Member States of the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO). In talks with the Tajik president, he said China will fully support Tajikistan in successfully hosting the SCO meeting, and stands ready to work with all parties to promote higher-quality development of the SCO. China is also willing to strengthen communication and coordination with Tajikistan within the United Nations, the China-Central Asia mechanism and other multilateral frameworks, actively implement the four global initiatives proposed by Chinese President Xi Jinping, and work together to build a community with a shared future for humanity, he said. The premier noted that China and Tajikistan are currently advancing efforts to build a community with a shared future between the two countries, and in May this year, President Xi met with President Rahmon, providing further guidance for the development of bilateral relations. China cherishes its profound friendship with Tajikistan and will always view China-Tajikistan relations from a strategic and long-term perspective, Li said. China stands ready to consolidate and deepen political mutual trust with Tajikistan, firmly support each other's core interests, continuously enhance the quality and effectiveness of cooperation, and continue to work hand in hand on the path toward modernization, he added. item.title: 5,300-square-meter flower display draws crowds in Xiamen
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
5,300-square-meter flower display draws crowds in Xiamen Photo shows an aerial view of a 5,300-square-meter flower display at Xiamen Horticulture Expo Garden in Jimei district, Xiamen, southeast China's Fujian Province. (People's Daily Online/Chen Bo) A vibrant sea of autumn flowers spanning 5,300 square meters is in full bloom on Haiyang Island at Xiamen Horticulture Expo Garden in Jimei district, Xiamen, southeast China's Fujian Province, attracting large numbers of visitors. More than 10 kinds of flowers bloom across the island, among them cockscombs, globe amaranths, Egyptian starclusters, begonias and Siam tulips. Red, yellow, orange, blue and pink stand out against green trees, clear water and open sky, with the city beyond. Visitors weave along the paths through the flower beds. Some stop to photograph the blooms, while others stroll on with family and friends. A visitor surnamed Wang, from Shenyang in northeast China's Liaoning Province, said she had made a point of visiting the flower display during her National Day trip to Xiamen after seeing it on social media. She said the blooms made her autumn sightseeing trip especially enjoyable, and that even her casual snapshots came out looking impressive. Colorful flower beds create a striking contrast with the surrounding buildings at Xiamen Horticulture Expo Garden in Jimei district, Xiamen, southeast China's Fujian Province. item.title: China's former revolutionary base areas embrace new chapter of development
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
China's former revolutionary base areas embrace new chapter of development Photo shows the Jiajin Mountain Tunnel in southwest China's Sichuan province. (Photo from People's Daily app) Two bridges over the Huajiang River in southwest China's Guizhou province offer a striking glimpse into the remarkable transformation of China's former revolutionary base areas. The first is the Huajiang Chain Bridge. With its iron chains and wooden-plank deck, it spans a section of the Beipan River. In 1935, as the Right-Flank Column of the Central Red Army advanced into southwestern Guizhou, the 11th Regiment of the Third Red Army Corps held its position here, buying precious time for the main force. This wartime lifeline embodied the determination to overcome every challenge and fight for victory. The other one, the Huajiang Grand Canyon Bridge, is pushing the boundaries of bridge construction in mountainous terrain through intelligent construction, innovative materials, advanced wind-resistant designs, and environmentally friendly building techniques. Its construction, which has set multiple world records, has effectively bridged the "gaps" created by the mountains and canyons. The old and new bridges now stand within sight of each other, offering a vivid picture of how former revolutionary base areas have changed, and Guizhou is far from the only example. The opening of flights at Ruijin Airport in east China's Jiangxi province has given people in southern Jiangxi and western Fujian, both former revolutionary base areas, a new "air corridor" linking them with the rest of the country. The Jiajin Mountain Tunnel in southwest China's Sichuan province has entered trial operation, turning the arduous journey "over" the mountain into a smooth passage "through" it and freeing local residents from worries about mountain closures caused by winter snow and ice. Bridges spanning valleys, passenger planes roaring overhead, and tunnels piercing through mountains -- the path to modernization for old revolutionary base areas is growing ever broader. Photo shows the Huajiang Grand Valley Bridge in southwest China's Guizhou province. (Photo/Li Yunfeng) What is driving these once-remote areas to take on a new look? Major undertakings call for riding the tide of the times. Development anchored in the prevailing trends of the era ensures the right direction and provides a strong driving force. That once-remote regions are no longer isolated, and less-developed areas no longer lag behind, owes much to their ability to seize opportunities of the times and align themselves with broader development trends. Deep in the mountains of Baisha township in Jishui county, Jiangxi province, fruit farmers are now able to sell their produce through livestreaming. This mountain hamlet, where people once "shouted to communicate and traveled on foot", is now equipped with 5G base stations, bringing new vitality to rural revitalization. Today, China boasts nearly 4.6 million 5G base stations and over 30.53 million gigabit-capable network ports, achieving gigabit-level connectivity for every county and 5G coverage in every township. From snow-capped mountains peaks to seashores, from the depth of dense forests to desert steppes, digital infrastructure functions like an intricate neural network, bridging the digital divide and bringing the benefits of digital and intelligent technologies to every corner of the country. For many regions, abundant resources and convenient locations offer a head start. Yet experience shows that the availability or scarcity of resources and other factors of production is never an absolute determinant. With the right approach and by building on their own strengths, regions can turn limitations into new advantages and cultivate new growth drivers from what they already have. During the Chinese People's War of Resistance Against Japanese Aggression, the people and soldiers of the Shaanxi-Gansu-Ningxia Border Region stepped up production to break the enemy's blockade, turning Qingyang in Gansu into the "granary of eastern Gansu." Today, Qingyang has once again taken stock of its strengths, drawing on its abundant energy resources and cool climate to develop data centers. Massive volumes of data can travel from Shanghai to the city in a matter of seconds, while computing power in Qingyang enables entrepreneurs in Guangdong in south China to render 3D models at high speed. As server lights replace oil lamps and streams of digital data flow across the land, data and computing power have become a new kind of "grain," helping drive local development while serving the needs of the country as a whole. Industrial upgrading and regional development both require a focus on local strengths and core industries, as well as openness to wider cooperation and integration. Photo shows the Huajiang Chain Bridge. (Photo from the official account of the media center of Zhenfeng county, Guizhou province on WeChat) The Fujian-Ningxia collaboration is a case in point. New forms of cooperation, such as "Fujian enterprises + Ningxia resources" and "Fujian headquarters + Ningxia production bases," are deepening and expanding. Freight trains under Ningxia's multimodal transport "single-document system," a system featuring one unified transport document covering the entire journey across different transport modes, carry full loads of goods bound for Fujian, Guangdong and beyond. Mountains and seas no longer stand as barriers. What began as one-way assistance has evolved into two-way mutual collaboration. Cross-regional reconfiguration of production factors has made regional cooperation more resilient and substantive. From the transformation of former revolutionary base areas to coordinated progress across regions, and from these changes to the steady and high-quality growth of China's economy, China is continuing along its Long March in the new era, moving forward with courage and opening up new horizons. item.title: Shenzhen ready to welcome APEC
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
Shenzhen ready to welcome APEC The atmosphere for the major APEC event builds in Shenzhen. (People's Daily Online/Wang Xing) The 33rd Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) Economic Leaders' Meeting will be held in Shenzhen, south China's Guangdong Province, on Nov. 18 and 19. It will be the third time China hosts the event. Shenzhen is stepping up preparations in areas ranging from border crossing and public services to public participation, aiming to make travel and daily life more convenient for delegates and international visitors. The Huanggang Port Joint Inspection Building begins operation. (People's Daily Online/Wang Xing) Upgraded ports of entry improve travel efficiency On Oct. 12, the redeveloped Huanggang Port, China's largest single port building and the world's largest land port complex, officially opened for operations. The port implements the colocation arrangement and the novel "collaborative inspection and joint clearance" mode, offering round-the-clock clearance services for cross-border passengers and vehicles. On its first day of operation, the facility handled 79,500 passenger crossings. Shenzhen Bao'an International Airport is piloting an advance screening procedure that has cut passenger entry clearance time during peak periods from 45 minutes to under 15 minutes. Nearly 400 new signs in Chinese, English, Japanese, Korean and other languages have also been installed. As of early September, the number of foreign passenger trips through the airport from APEC member economies this year had exceeded one million, a record for the same period. The airport operates more than 30 passenger routes to key APEC cities, with over 700 inbound and outbound flights scheduled each week. Photo shows a Chinese-English public sign in Shenzhen. (People's Daily Online/Wang Xing) Better services make Shenzhen more accessible to international visitors Shenzhen is continuing to improve services for international visitors, including foreign-language signage, transportation, payment and tax refunds. Effective Oct. 1, regulations on the standardized use and management of foreign-language public signs set out requirements for signage in eight categories of public places, helping create a more accessible language environment. More than 7,000 smart translation devices have been deployed at bus and subway stations, government service halls, cultural venues and sports facilities across Shenzhen. Over 5,000 taxis are equipped with AI-powered devices that support real-time voice translation in more than 140 languages. English names are available at all 11,000 bus stops across the city, and passengers can scan QR codes on bus-stop signs to access route information in English and real-time arrival updates. For payments, all 17 metro lines and 432 stations in the city accept contactless payments with overseas bank cards. As of July, 41,000 merchants across the city accepted overseas bank cards, supported by 51,000 point-of-sale terminals. From January to August, foreign nationals made 143 million transactions in Shenzhen, totaling 21.09 billion yuan ($3.15 billion), up 18.64 percent and 26.58 percent year on year, respectively. Shenzhen is also expanding services such as departure tax refunds and currency exchange at its airport and in commercial districts. Hospitals, hotels, tourist attractions and legal service providers are working to improve their services for international visitors and clients. Shenzhen residents sign their names on a signature board to show support for green mobility. (People's Daily Online/Wang Xing) Residents join preparations to welcome the Asia-Pacific gathering On Oct. 15, Shenzhen launched a green mobility initiative encouraging residents to reduce or suspend private car use during APEC meeting week. Within three hours of the initiative's launch, more than 20,000 car owners had registered to keep their vehicles off the road. By the morning of Oct. 17, the number had exceeded 230,000. Fourteen universities in Shenzhen, including Shenzhen University and the Southern University of Science and Technology, have established volunteer teams for APEC-related services. International volunteers are active in markets and communities, while student volunteers from Shenzhen Foreign Languages School have been helping foreign visitors navigate Shenzhen North Railway Station and answering their questions. Civil servants are also taking part in safety inspections at the community level, promoting orderly traffic, guiding visitors at venues and supporting international exchange activities. Freight drivers have formed a city volunteer service team, while couriers and food delivery riders are attending classes to learn basic foreign languages and protocol for interacting with international visitors. From border clearance and everyday public services to green mobility and volunteer assistance, Shenzhen is continuing to improve its international services as it prepares to host the APEC meeting. item.title: Inside China's "unlikely" AI computing hub
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-19
Inside China's "unlikely" AI computing hub A drone photo taken on Sept. 10, 2026 shows a cloud computing center of VNET Group in Ulanqab, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Li Zhipeng) HOHHOT, Oct. 18 (Xinhua) -- A four-hour drive northwest of Beijing takes one across the Great Wall and into the grasslands of Inner Mongolia, seemingly a world away from China's booming coastal towns. Yet here, in a city once known as China's "potato capital," data centers are rising from the grasslands, towering cranes fill the skyline, and some of the country's biggest tech companies are moving in. The city is Ulanqab, in the Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, which has emerged as a new frontier in the global race for computing power. Ulanqab is a poster child for this rise. In less than two years, Inner Mongolia's computing capacity has nearly quadrupled, reaching 363,000 petaflops by August 2026, as large-scale data centers have sprung up across the region. A combination of factors helped fuel this transformation. Its climate allows natural cooling of AI server racks for nearly ten months a year. The windswept steppes offer a massive volume of wind and solar power, driving rates down to as low as around 0.35 yuan (about 5.2 U.S. cents) per kWh. Moreover, its proximity to Beijing ensures an ultra-low latency of under 5 milliseconds, facilitating seamless model training and real-time inference. A staff member checks the computing power equipment at a supercomputing technology company in the Horinger New Area of Hohhot, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, June 4, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Zhipeng) However, the region is not content to remain a mere "landlord of data centers." It is striving to move up the value chain, reinventing itself not only as a hub for green computing but also for token trading and AI applications. RISING ABOVE GRASSLAND At the Ulanqab Chahar High Tech Development Zone, the epicenter of the city's newfound buzz, an "Apple Boulevard" runs alongside an "Alibaba Boulevard" and a "Huawei Boulevard" -- named after three of the major companies that have set up a presence here. Other tech giants, including ByteDance, Kuaishou and VNET Group, have also moved in. Vehicles from across China line the roads, and workers speak in accents from every corner of the country. Around lunchtime, food stalls spring up around the construction sites, selling boxed meals, fruit and drinks. "Within the high-tech zone alone, 22 computing-power projects are currently under construction, involving nearly 30,000 construction workers," said Liu Junping, deputy director of the administrative committee of the development zone. "When I came here to scout the site in 2022, it was still pretty desolate, and sandstorms would sometimes sweep through," recalled Zhou Yiguang, an executive with the VNET Group's Ulanqab base. The group has planned a computing cluster covering 1,100 mu (about 73 hectares) of land in Ulanqab, and the first phase has been in operation since October 2024. A drone photo taken on Sept. 10, 2026 shows the construction site of a new cloud computing center of VNET Group in Ulanqab, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Li Zhipeng) In fact, it is not just Ulanqab. Inner Mongolia has emerged as a hub for computing power, with its regional capital Hohhot as another high ground. As of the first half of 2026, roughly 20 of China's 30 leading private computing companies had established a presence in the region, with combined investment exceeding 200 billion yuan (around 29.75 billion U.S. dollars). In addition, nine of the country's top 10 computing service providers had also set up operations there. GREEN COMPUTING With the influx comes new challenges. Computing facilities require enormous amounts of electricity to run and water to keep server racks from overheating. Inner Mongolia, a frontrunner in China's green energy transition, is charting a course of green computing. In 2025, the computing industry in Ulanqab alone consumed 4.3 billion kWh of electricity. That figure is estimated to reach 9 billion kWh in 2026 and will continue to surge as more computing centers are expected to start operating over the next two to three years. An aerial drone photo taken on June 4, 2026 shows a wind-photovoltaic power storage station of Huadian (Inner Mongolia) New Energy Co., Ltd. as part of the Horinger data center cluster green energy supply demonstration project, in Hohhot, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region. (Xinhua/Li Zhipeng) Globally, tech giants are moving beyond simply "buying power" to "competing for power" and even "generating their own power." China, however, has leveraged its world-leading power grid, renewable energy and energy storage industries to pioneer the integration of computing power and electricity supply, known as "computing-electricity coordination." In the Ulanqab Chahar High Tech Development Zone, a zero-carbon industrial park is taking shape. The park will be managed as a unified power distribution unit, with wind and solar infrastructure developed collectively by the government, then distributed to individual computing centers across the park. Chen Zhigang, deputy director of the Ulanqab municipal development and reform commission, said that the park's surrounding areas have about 10 gigawatts of wind and solar development capacity available. Once tapped, these resources could generate more than 30 billion kWh of electricity annually, enough to cover future increases in demand. After the zero-carbon industrial park is completed, more than 80 percent of the park's electricity will come directly from renewable energy. In the Horinger New Area in Hohhot, computing centers in operation source 85 percent of their power consumption from green energy. Water poses another potential constraint. However, widespread adoption of water-conserving cooling equipment, such as waterless fluorine-pump air conditioning systems and closed cooling towers, helped ease the high demand for cooling water. Moreover, take VNET Group's cloud computing center in Ulanqab for example: here, outdoor cold air is directly used for cooling for nearly 10 months of the year, with spray systems activated only during the hottest summer days. "All the water used for cooling at the computing center is reclaimed water. It does not affect local natural water resources or groundwater," said Li Yi, technical director of VNET Group's Ulanqab base. According to the Ulanqab water resources bureau, under the regional regulations, data centers are prohibited from using groundwater as cooling water. In 2025, big data companies across the city consumed 1.54 million cubic meters of water, accounting for only 0.33 percent of the city's total water consumption. Meanwhile, the city produces about 72 million tonnes of reclaimed water annually. TOKEN HUB Building computing capacity is one thing, yet turning it into a high-value AI economy is another. "If we rely solely on cheap electricity and low land costs, we risk becoming little more than 'landlords of server rooms,'" Liu Huansuo, deputy director of the Ulanqab big data administration, warned. The concern is well-founded. The high-value segments of the computing economy -- chips, algorithms and models -- remain largely beyond Inner Mongolia's reach. According to economic data from Ulanqab, the city's computing-power industry generated 6.835 billion yuan in revenue in 2025, with 368 million yuan in tax revenue. A computing center is estimated to create about 100 jobs per 100 mu (about 6.7 hectares) of land. Yet these returns remain modest relative to the massive upfront investment in infrastructure and the enormous computing capacity that is being developed. Staff members operate the multi-cloud computing power resource monitoring and scheduling platform of Horinger data center cluster to monitor in real time and dynamically schedule computing power resources, at a talent and innovation valley in the Horinger New Area of Hohhot, north China's Inner Mongolia Autonomous Region, June 4, 2026. (Xinhua/Li Zhipeng) To address the challenge, Inner Mongolia strives to move up the value chain -- evolving from a "server-room landlord" to a "token capital," and cultivating its own ecosystem of AI applications. On May 30, Inner Mongolia's Token Trading Platform, billed as the country's first green-computing full-stack AI platform, went into operation in the Horinger New Area, positioning Hohhot to become a major token-trading hub in northern China. The goal is to turn raw computing power into a tradable commodity that can be measured, priced and ultimately converted into higher-value AI services, said Guo Juying, deputy director of the Horinger New Area Administrative Committee. She described the transition as a shift from "selling electricity" to "selling tokens," as every AI conversation or model inference can ultimately be measured in terms of tokens generated and consumed. Ulanqab has its own plan. At the end of 2025, the city released a three-year action plan for building a "Token Capital" for 2026-2028, envisioning a new economic chain spanning the production, trading and application of tokens. The application ecosystem is also expanding. Hohhot has developed nearly 100 application scenarios in sectors such as dairy, new energy and biomedicine. A facial recognition database for cattle is already widely used on smart pastures. For a region that has built its computing infrastructure at remarkable speed, the next challenge may be harder. But overcoming it will open up a whole new horizon across China's economic landscape. Copyright © 2026 People's Daily Online. All Rights Reserved.
